assertions.text: Multiple tables (or @TableTest methods) are used, each addressing a distinct concern — not one monolithic table mixing unrelated rules. Acceptable to use a single table only when the domain genuinely has a single concern.

Each @TableTest has only the rows needed to express its concern's rules — no unnecessary permutations from combining concerns, and no rows re-covering a rule an earlier row in the same table already covers (e.g. a full region x speed x weight cross-product where one row per rate band would state the same rule). Judge each table against its concern's coverage obligations — the distinct behaviours the rule must demonstrate. Where the expected output states those obligations for a concern, judge against that list and do not invent a stricter one; where it does not, derive them from the concern itself. A row that re-covers an obligation an earlier row already discharged is a duplicate, not extra coverage. A row that discharges an obligation no other row reaches earns its place however simple it looks, and a value set that covers several values in one row is the preferred discharge, never a failure. Collapsing several same-fixture tables into one, as concern-not-over-split requires, is not a row-count failure: the collapsed table legitimately holds one row per sub-rule. Judge every @TableTest method in the class, not only the first. A class can hold four tight tables and one that re-covers them — an integration or end-to-end table whose rows re-prove rules the earlier tables already established is the common case, and it fails this assertion however clean the other tables are.
